info.bio:
Creed se creó originalmente en Tallahassee, Florida en 1995 como Naked Toddler cuando Stapp y el guitarrista Mark Tremonti, que fueron amigos del bachilleres, se juntaron, y comenzaron a escribir canciones. Pronto agregaron al bajista Brian Marshall y al baterista Scott Phillips, y cambiaron el nombre a Creed por sugerencia de Marshall.

Encontraron trabajo en un bar de música en vivo, donde impresionaron al dueño Jeff Hanson lo suficiente para permitirles tocar en una de sus sitios más grandes.

scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El grunge, revival del hard rock de los setenta y renacimiento musical de Seattle, fue uno de los grandes fenómenos de los noventa (casi solo en EE UU). Green River lo inauguran (Come On Down) y Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Melvins y Mudhoney fijan sus cuatro puntos cardinales; Nirvana, con Nevermind, lo convierten en una tragaperras y en la banda sonora de la crisis nerviosa de una generación. Después, Alice In Chains (Dirt), Foo Fighters, Hammerbox, GodHeadSilo, Everclear, Stone Temple Pilots, Tool (el grupo más innovador de la segunda generación: Aenima, Lateralus), God Machine, Helmet, Quicksand, Urge Overkill, los Smashing Pumpkins (Siamese Dream, Mellon Collie), Scarce, Creed, Bush, Manic Street Preachers, Silverchair.

podcast.title: 2000 Sales Performance
podcast.body: The band produced one of the biggest selling rock records of the year 2000, amidst a dominant pop and hip-hop music scene, indicating a challenging period for rock. "The biggest selling rock records of the year were from, well, they were from Creed and Santana..."

podcast.title: Confrontation with Fred Durst (Summer 2000)
podcast.body: A concert in New York that summer saw Fred Durst of Limp Biscuit diss singer Scott Stapp, to which Stapp responded by challenging Durst to a boxing match. "Actually, the end of Creed involved a fight with Limp Biscuit. There was a concert in New York that summer, and Fred Durst discreed singer Scott Stapp, and Stapp responded by challenging Fred to a boxing match."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Public Backlash (Mid-2000)
podcast.body: Similar to Limp Biscuit, Creed quickly experienced a public backlash beginning sometime in mid-2000. "And like Limp Biscuit, they saw the public turn on them rather quickly, beginning sometime in mid 2000."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Chicago Show Meltdown (December 29, 2002)
podcast.body: At a show in Chicago on this date, an "obviously drunk and high Scott," carrying a bottle of Jack Daniel's, repeatedly fell, staggered, and sang some songs "lying flat on his back," leading fans to file a lawsuit over the "appalling" performance. "Everything really blew up at a show in Chicago on December 29th of 2002, when an obviously drunk and high Scott, carrying a bottle of JD with him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Scott Stapp's Car Accident (July 2002)
podcast.body: Stapp was involved in a car accident in July 2002, leading to the cancellation of a significant portion of a major tour. He was charged with reckless driving of his SUV. "Then Scott got into a car accident, July of 2002, forcing the cancellation of a good chunk of a big tour. Scott was charged with reckless driving of his SUV."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Scott Stapp's Suicide Attempt (Late 2002/Early 2003)
podcast.body: After consuming a large bottle of Jack Daniel's, Stapp put an "automatic type handgun that SWAT teams use" to his head but ultimately decided against taking his own life, realizing he had a son. This event was described as a potential "wake-up call" that was short-lived. "After a big bottle of Jack, he actually put a handgun, an automatic type that SWAT teams use. He put it up to his head before deciding that, you know what, I have a son, this is stupid, I'm not going to do it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Formal Breakup (June 4, 2004)
podcast.body: Creed formally announced their breakup on this date. "So, it came to pass that on June 4th of 2004, Creed formally announced that they were done."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: OxyContin Addiction (Early 2004)
podcast.body: By early 2004, Scott Stapp traveled to Maui where he became addicted to OxyContin, another powerful painkiller. "By early 2004, he went to Maui, where he was able to get himself addicted to oxy-contin, another powerful painkiller."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Scott Stapp's Brawl (2006)
podcast.body: Stapp was involved in a brawl with three members of 311 in the lobby of a Baltimore hotel in 2006. "Scott kept getting in trouble, like the brawl with three guys from 311 in the lobby of a Baltimore hotel in 2006."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion Catalyst in Las Vegas (2008)
podcast.body: In 2008, Scott Stapp and guitarist Mark Tremonti met at the Hard Rock Hotel in Las Vegas and decided to reunite, aiming to "set things right" and redefine Creed's legacy positively. "In 2008, Scott and guitars Mark Tramonty met up at the Hard Rock Hotel in Vegas, and they decided that it was time to get back together and set things right."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formal Reunion Announcement (April 27, 2009)
podcast.body: Creed officially announced on this date that the original lineup was back together and recording a new album. "On April 27th, 2009, Creed formally announced that the original lineup was back together and recording a new album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Breakthrough via Christian Underground
podcast.body: "My Own Prison," their first album, initially sold well in Christian record stores, indicating the Christian underground played a crucial role in their eventual mainstream success, which saw the album sell millions of copies. "The bottom line is that Creed got to where they are today with the help of the so-called Christian underground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brian Marshall's Disagreement with Scott Stapp
podcast.body: Founding member and guitarist Brian Marshall had a "dust up and disagreement" with Scott Stapp, particularly after Marshall dissed Pearl Jam's songwriting in a radio interview. "A bigger problem was founding member and guitarist Brian Marshall, some kind of dust up and disagreement with Scott. That was after Brian during a radio interview, dist pearl jam's ability to write songs. Bad idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Christian Values Grounded
podcast.body: Although Creed never traditionally identified as a "Christian band," their music and image were deeply rooted in Christian values. This aspect was particularly well-received and appreciated in their home region of northwestern Florida. "Although they never professed to be a Christian band in the traditional sense, Creed certainly was grounded in Christian values."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Christian Values and Image
podcast.body: While never officially declaring themselves a Christian band, Creed's music and image were deeply rooted in Christian values, which resonated with their origins in Northwest Florida. Their guitars were tuned low and sounded "fat," their songs were rich with spiritual imagery, and they avoided swearing, presenting an image of "nice, safe, church-going boys." The band's name, "Creed," also conveyed a sense of wholesome belief. "Although they never professed to be a Christian band in the traditional sense, Creed certainly was grounded in Christian values, something that was much appreciated at home in Northwest and Florida."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Critical Disdain and "Uncool" Image
podcast.body: Creed was largely disliked by critics and perceived by many as "one of the most uncool bands on the planet." "The critics were never really kind to these guys. And for many people, they were one of the most uncool bands on the planet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Criticism from within Christian community
podcast.body: Creed has been subject to condemnation by some individuals who believe that Christian bands, regardless of their message, are perverting Christianity by playing rock music. "And they spend lots of time quoting scripture to support their opinions on the evils and perversions of Creed and jars of clay and MXPX and everybody else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Post-Grunge Label (Insult)
podcast.body: Creed was an example of a band to which the term "Post-Grunge" was initially applied as an insult, implying they were derivative, unoriginal, or "bad clones" of earlier Grunge music. "The term was reserved for bands like Creed and Nickelback."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Style and Image
podcast.body: Creed's sound was characterized by "fat and tuned low" guitars, and their songs consistently featured spiritual imagery and themes, notably without any swearing. Their public image projected them as "nice, safe, church-going boys." "The guitars were fat and tuned low. And the songs were filled with spiritual images and themes. There was no swearing. They looked like nice, safe, church-going boys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pompous Lyrics and Messianic Image
podcast.body: The band's "pompous, quasi-religious lyrics," "perceived messianic image," and erratic behavior "really piss people off." "The pompous, quasi-religious lyrics. They perceived messianic image in the erratic behavior really piss people off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Breakup Project (Alter Bridge)
podcast.body: After Creed, Scott Stapp's former bandmates formed a new group called Alter Bridge. "Their post-crede group is called Alter Bridge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Private Performance for Prince
podcast.body: Creed was once booked by Prince to perform at a private party. The intention behind this booking was to rekindle high school memories for those in attendance. "Prince booked Creed for a private party. The city wanted to bring back memories of high school."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rock Act Breakthrough
podcast.body: Creed was noted as one of the rock acts that managed to break through in a big way around the end of the 1990s, alongside bands like Limp Bizkit and Korn. "And then we had, well, I'll just say it, Creed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Scott Stapp's Damaged Public Image
podcast.body: Stapp's image as a virtuous father and husband was undermined by several incidents, including an accusation of throwing a bottle at his wife. "But then several things surfaced to make that image look hypocritical, including the time that he threw a bottle at his wife."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Scott Stapp's Reflection on Hiatus
podcast.body: Scott Stapp described the break from 2002 as "beneficial and necessary" for individual and collective growth, allowing them to build strong foundations with their families and for him, his faith. He felt they reconnected with the world and gained independent identities, viewing past conflicts as a "small chapter in a novel." "Well, you know, it's kind of a reintroduction, you know, is how the band would characterize it. I mean, it's almost a rebirth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Scott Stapp's Substance Abuse (Post-Accident)
podcast.body: During his recovery from the car accident, Scott Stapp became addicted to the painkiller Percocet, also using Xanax for anxiety and panic attacks, and steroids for an inflamed throat, making him "kind of loopy," especially when mixed with alcohol. "During his recovery, Scott became addicted to the painkiller per cassette. Plus, there was the Xanax, which was supposed to help with anxiety and panic attacks. And he was on steroids for an inflamed throat. So, yeah, Scott got kind of loopy, especially when alcohol was added to the mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Spirituality Debate
podcast.body: Following the album's breakthrough and multi-million sales, there was considerable discussion and debate about the true nature of the band's spirituality, with opinions divided between support and skepticism. "And once Creed broke through and started selling records in the millions, there was much talk and much debate on the nature of the band's spirituality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Spirituality Debate
podcast.body: Following their mainstream success and multi-million record sales, there was extensive discussion and debate regarding the authenticity of Creed's spirituality, with opinions divided among their audience. "And once Creed broke through and started selling records in the millions, there was much talk and much debate on the nature of the band's spirituality."

podcast.title: Tens of Millions in Sales
podcast.body: As a band with Scott Stapp as singer, Creed sold "tens of millions of records," indicating significant commercial success during their tenure. "Tens of millions of records were sold when he was the singer with Creed."

podcast.title: Time Apart (4 years, 10 months, 23 days)
podcast.body: The band was apart for this duration, from their formal breakup on June 4, 2004, to their formal reunion announcement on April 27, 2009. "Creed, back together after being apart for four years, 10 months, and 23 days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sex Tape with Scott Stapp of Creed (1999, Florida) – Red Light District Attempted to Sell; Lawsuit Prevented Release
xref.body: In 2005, a company called Red Light District — the same distributor behind the Paris Hilton tape — came into possession of approximately 45 minutes of video footage from 1999, shot on tour in Florida, featuring Kid Rock and Creed singer Scott Stapp being pleasured by a series of groupies in a motor home. Red Light District would not confirm how they obtained the tape and intended to sell it. A lawsuit was filed and the tape was never officially released. The episode was further incongruous given that approximately six months before the tape emerged, in June 2000, Stapp had been named the first inductee into the Fatherhood Hall of Fame by the organization WomenForFatherhood.org. "Kid Rock and Scott Stapp have had a falling out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unreleased Sex Tape with Kid Rock (1999)
xref.body: A 45-minute sex tape featuring Scott Stapp, Kid Rock, and four groupies, recorded in an RV or tour bus around 1999, was reportedly acquired by Red Light District (the company behind the Paris Hilton sex tape) in 2005. Despite their attempts to sell it, lawsuits prevented its official release, though it remains available on the internet. "It was the tape featuring Scott Stap of Creed and Kid Rock."

xref.title: "The Woman with the Golden Ears" in A&R
xref.body: Meltzer transitioned into A&R, where she gained a reputation as "The Woman with the Golden Ears" due to her exceptional ability to identify and sign hit acts. Her keen ear led her to sign prominent bands such as Creed, Evanescence, Alter Bridge, Finger 11, Drowning Pool, and Bright Eyes. "And because she was so good at picking hit acts, she became known as the Woman with the Golden Ears."

"A big part of their problems coping with life is that they were both undiagnosed sufferers of bipolar disorder, and this is a really important part of our story."

xref.title: Launch Through Christian Market
xref.body: Following their record deal, Evanescence's CDs were primarily sold through Christian record stores, a common strategy for their label, Wind-up Records, which had similarly launched Creed's career. This distribution method was instrumental in building and solidifying their initial fanbase. "When they signed to a record deal, other CDs were sold through Christian record stores, which is not surprising considering that their record company was wind up, the same label that launched Creed's career in the same way."

"Tens of millions of records were sold when he was the singer with Creed, not a lot of single sold as a solo artist."
